description:
Basil Beebalm (Monarda clinopodioides)

22 May 2016
Ray Roberts Lake State Park - Isle Du Bois
Pilot Point, Denton County, Texas

A native wildflower, Basil Beebalm grows in a limited area of the United States including only four states (listed alphabetically): Kansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas. Images 3 and 4 show four new plants of Basil Beebalm growing amid another of a Black-eyed Susan that are about to bloom. Because of its occurrence in North America, Basil Beebalm is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. Ray Roberts Lake State Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

26 June 2016 
Lyndon B. Johnson National Grassland 
County Road 2560 & Forest Service Road 900 
Wise County, Texas

Spotted Horse Mint was abundant sporadically throughout the trail. Spotted Horse Mint is a quintessentially North American wildflower. Additional common names or alternate spelllings for Spotted Horse Mint include Spotted Beebalm, Spotted Horsemint and Horsemint. Here's the thumbnail sketch for this wildflower at the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center: "An aromatic, erect perennial ranging from only 6 in. to almost 3 ft. tall. Rosettes of yellowish, purple-spotted, tubular flowers occur in whorls, forming a dense, elongated spike at the end of the stem or from leaf axils. Each whorl is subtended by large, conspicuous, whitish, purple-tinged, leaf-like bracts. Linnaeus named the genus Monarda in honor of a 16th century Spanish physician and botanist, Nicolas Bautista Monardes (1493-1588). Monardes never went to the Americas but was able to study medicinal plants in Spain because Spain controlled navigation and commerce from the New World." Its extensive range begins in a line east from New Mexico to Wisconsin (in the U.S.), and from Ontario and Québec east to Hudson Bay and the Atlantic Ocean, and because of its occurrence in Texas counties bordering with Mexico, it is clearly present in Mexico's northeast, where its farthest southern range appears to occur. Because of its North American range, Spotted Horse Mint is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The Lyndon B. Johnson National Grassland is administered by the US Forest Service, US Department of Agriculture.

Sources:

I am focusing my attention to the purple flower in the middle of the mess of Indian Blankets. This purple flower is very pretty. It is a stack of multiple buds and things. It almost reminds me of that Spotted Horse Mint that I found at the this same area. This plant was very interesting and was mainly pink or more a light lavender color and was only as tall as the Indian Blankets. It had little pinkish puce leaves. It was a very interesting wildflower.

This patch was attracting many wasps and other insects.

description:
"Wild bergamot was considered a medicinal plant by many Native Americans including the Menominee, the Ojibwe, and the Winnebago (Ho-Chunk). It was used most commonly to treat colds, and was frequently made into a tea. Today, many families still use wild bergamot during the cold and flu season. The tea may be sweetened with honey, as it tends to be quite strong.[17]

The species of Monarda that may go under the common name "bee balm," including M. fistulosa, have a long history of use as a medicinal plant by Native Americans, including the Blackfoot. The Blackfoot recognized the plant's strong antiseptic action, and used poultices of the plant for skin infections and minor wounds.[citation needed] A tea made from the plant was also used to treat mouth and throat infections caused by dental caries and gingivitis.[citation needed] Bee balm is the natural source of the antiseptic thymol, the primary active ingredient in modern commercial mouthwash formulas. The Winnebago used a tea made from bee balm as a general stimulant.[citation needed] Bee balm was also used as a carminative herb by Native Americans to treat excessive flatulence.[18] Leaves were eaten boiled with meat and a concoction of the plant was made into hair pomade. The herb is considered an active diaphoretic (sweat inducer).

The essential oil of Monarda fistulosa was analyzed using mass spectrometry and arithmetical retention indices, and was found to contain p-cymene (32.5%), carvacrol (24.0%), thymol (12.6%), an aliphatic aldehyde (6.3%), the methyl ether of carvacrol (5.5%), α-pinene (3.5%), β-pinene (2.9%), sabinene hydrate (1.9%), α-terpinene (1.7%), citronellyl acetate (1.6%), and β-caryophyllene (1.1%)."
